title: Week 8 — What Salesforce exam day is actually like (14 exams in)

mediaNotes.carousel: 4–6 slides: Webassessor check-in steps (room scan, ID, login buffer)

tweets:
I've taken 14 Salesforce certification exams.

the first one I nearly failed the check-in before the test started.

here's what exam day is actually like

a thread

#SalesforceCertification

you take it from your computer via Kryterion Webassessor.

Live proctor watches via webcam the whole time.

They'll ask you to show the room, clear your desk. They take it seriously.

Clear your space the night before.

Check-in takes 15-20 min.

Log in at your exact time = already behind.

Log in 30 min early. Every time.

Test webcam/mic night before — a last-minute tech issue is the worst start.

Biggest first-timer trap: question wording.

SF never asks 'right answer?'

It asks BEST approach / MOST appropriate / LEAST likely to cause issues.

Two answers can be correct. Only one is the Salesforce way.

Stuck on a Q?
1. Cross out the two obviously wrong.
2. Of remaining: more declarative/native?
3. Better for data integrity?
4. Still stuck? Mark & move on.

Never >90s first pass. Come back fresh.

the night before: do one practice exam, clear your desk, check your login.

that's it.

no new material. no cramming. if you don't know it by the night before, two more hours won't save you.

sleep is more useful than one more Trailhead module at 11pm.

if you fail:
Get score report (weak sections).
Breathe. Then study ONLY those — don't restart everything.

retake timing bites — Webassessor + score report (first retake ≠ later sits). don't parrot one-liners from X. the wait is mental too.

series.label: ADM-201 traps that still eat people in 2026

a thread

#ADM201 #SalesforceFlow

before-save vs after-save isn't trivia.

before-save runs in the same database transaction as the save. good for field updates that have to happen *before* validation finishes its job.

after-save = you already committed. different constraints.

record-triggered flow that updates the *same* record that fired it — safe vs recursive nightmare fuel.

cross-object write after stage change? formula won't update the related record. flow will.

happy-path builds won't teach that — practice qs will.

scheduled paths vs record-triggered.

scheduled = clock / batch-ish mental model.

record-triggered = something happened to a row, react now (with entry conditions). stems usually telegraph which one they want.

subflows aren't just 'cleaner.'

sometimes they're the right answer because you reuse the same chunk from three places and the scenario says maintainability / duplication.

the exam cares about that wording.

autolaunched vs screen flow.

screen = human in the loop.

autolaunched = something else kicked it off. if the question has a user clicking 'next,' it's not autolaunched. sounds obvious. people still miss it cold.

title: Spring '26 Release — Human voice rewrite
notes: Do NOT add headers or bullet points. Each tweet should feel like a separate thought, not a slide in a deck. Post as a thread.
tweets:
Spring '26 is out.

every 4 months Salesforce updates every single org on the planet at the same time. no warning. no 'are you ready?' it just happens.

if you work in Salesforce and you're not paying attention to releases, you're flying blind.

here's what you actually need to know about this one
a thread

#Spring26 #Salesforce #SalesforceOhana

first — if you're new to Salesforce and confused about what a 'release' even is:

most software has versions. Salesforce doesn't. there's no v8.3 your company is stuck on while everyone else has v9.

there's just Salesforce. and three times a year — Winter, Spring, Summer — it updates. for everyone. everywhere. at the same time.

no other major enterprise platform does it this way. it's genuinely unusual.

and yes, the naming makes no sense.

Winter '26 dropped in October.
Spring '26 dropped in February.
Summer '26 will drop around June.

Winter in October.

I've been in this ecosystem for years and it still makes me do a double take every time. you get used to it.

the part that trips people up most: you do get a heads up.

before a release hits your production org, it lands in your sandbox first — usually 3-4 weeks early.

most admins don't check. then something breaks in production after the release and they spend two days debugging a Flow that worked fine last month.

the sandbox preview exists. use it. 30 minutes of testing saves a lot of pain.

so what actually changed in Spring '26 that's worth your attention:

Agentforce can now orchestrate multiple agents. meaning one agent can hand off to another mid-conversation based on context.

if you haven't started paying attention to Agentforce yet — this is the release where it starts becoming something you have to know for both your job and your cert exams.

Flow got new debugging tools.

this sounds boring. it's not.

anyone who's spent 3 hours staring at a Flow that fails silently with zero useful error messages knows exactly why this matters.

the new debugging in Spring '26 is one of those updates that sounds like a minor QoL thing but will save you real time.

Data Cloud got heavier on identity resolution and real-time data activation.

if you're on any project that touches Data Cloud, the way customer profiles are unified and activated changed. not broken — improved. but different enough that documentation from 6 months ago may not match what you're seeing now.

the certification angle — because I know why most of you are reading this:

exam outlines update with releases. if you're studying from a course that hasn't been touched since last year, parts of it are wrong or irrelevant now.

the official Salesforce exam guide on Trailhead is always current. it's free. and it's more accurate than most paid courses. check that first.

also: if you're already certified, Spring '26 opens your maintenance exam window.

maintenance exams are 30-40 questions on what changed in the release. most people dread them.

honestly they're the least painful thing about holding a Salesforce cert. 30 minutes, focused on the new stuff you should probably know anyway. just do them when the window opens.

the things Spring '26 didn't change:

OWD, roles, profiles, permission sets. governor limits. Flow fundamentals. the sharing model.

those have been the backbone of this platform for 15+ years and they're not going anywhere.

if you're prepping for any Salesforce exam — those concepts are still 40-60% of your score. Spring '26 didn't touch them.

last thing:

Salesforce releases 500+ pages of release notes every cycle. nobody reads them all. not even the people writing them probably.

but the highlights take about 20 minutes to get through. worth doing once per release just to know what landed.

most people answer with a happy story.

interviewers hear that every day.

the version that works better:

pick a real messy situation. explain the pressure, the constraint, and the decision you made.

then say what you’d do differently now.

lesson: document the technical debt the same day you ship.

title: How I study for Salesforce exams without burning out

i used to study 4–5 hours a night.

now I study 90 focused minutes and score higher.

here’s the actual system.

a thread

#SalesforceCertification

rule 1: stop when the marginal gain drops.

after 90–110 minutes, most people are just re-reading what they already know. that’s not studying. that’s performing.

rule 2: active recall > passive review.

close the notes. write the question from memory. then check.

the gap between what you think you know and what you can actually recall is where the points live.

rule 3: one topic per session.

not “study admin.” pick one sub-topic (e.g., before-save vs after-save flows) and go deep for 45 minutes.

breadth feels productive. depth moves the score.

- rewatching the same Trailhead module
- highlighting everything
- passive note-taking without testing myself
- studying when I’m already mentally done

then stop. even if you feel like you could do more.
